A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, wholly. Grey. Far.

2463456.twitter_share_message: “Joyce here makes no illusions about Bloom’s religion and about his awareness of the horrors of W…” —@Genius

children: Joyce here makes no illusions about Bloom’s religion and about his awareness of the horrors of World War I, and the horrors previously visited upon Jewish people, evoking Sodom and Gomorrah, both consumed by Yahweh’s fire and brimstone, on the edge of the dead sea, and now dead names, uncertain even to have ever existed.

Bloom is reminded of the ancient Jewish people by an elderly woman bent double, clutching a naggin of some spirits, and thinks on the traumas visited upon Jewish people, their births and deaths in captivity, musing on the dual meaning of ‘bear’, that they can suffer no more these traumas, that the elderly, broken woman can bear no more children.
PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I would also mention that this may be a similar time to when Stephen witnesses the same event in Telemachus:
“A cloud began to cover the sun slowly, shadowing the bay behind him in deeper green.”
The event appears to produce a similar effect in the minds of both men, which is then followed by an uplifting feel when the sunlight returns.

children: Is this true? Let’s let
The Straight Dope
take this one away. First of all, it’s
white
clothing that reflects sunlight–but there’s a catch:
White clothing reflects sunlight, but also reflects internal heat back towards your body, so the net effect under identical conditions is less cooling than if you wore black.
Black clothing actually keeps you cooler, for reasons related to wind speed:
…black clothing absorbs sunlight and the heat radiating from your body, but if it is loose-fitting, and there is wind, the wind convects the heat away faster than it is absorbed.
The full breakdown is here.
By the way,
refraction

of light is something totally different–that’s when light waves change direction due to a change in transmission medium, as from air to water. It’s what causes objects half-in, half-out of water to appear broken or distorted:
Bottom line: Bloom’s a smart guy, but he’s a little off base on this one.

4724200.fragment: Somewhere in the east: early morning: set off at dawn. Travel round in front of the sun, steal a day’s march on him. Keep it up for ever never grow a day older technically.

range.content: Somewhere in the east: early morning: set off at dawn. Travel round in front of the sun, steal a day's march on him. Keep it up for ever never grow a day older technically.

4724200.twitter_share_message: “If one sets off from Troy, and attempts to outpace the sun, one must be travelling west, as Ulys…” —@Genius

children: If one sets off from Troy, and attempts to outpace the sun, one must be travelling west, as Ulysses would have initially been on his journey home to Ithaca. We know, of course, that after the big storm that pushed them well off course to the Land of the Lotus Eaters, Ulysses and his men were well to the west of Ithaca. Events then pushed them farther northwest until they arrived at the Land of the Dead (quite possibly Monaco), some 1,100 miles west of home: a great distance even by today’s car and ferry.
Monaco

From there, staying ahead of the sun on his way home wouldn’t make sense – unless the appearance on its headpiece of the sun rising from the northwest behind the Bank of Ireland in the risible attempt at nationalism by the newspaper for which Bloom sold advertising, the Freeman Leader, weren’t astronomically absurd.

In that case, if one were passing, say Thrinacia, home of sun god/cattleman Helios, and had been warned by goddess of magic, Circe, as well as the spirit of blind prophet, Tiresius, to avoid the place, one’s judgment and strength of character might be called into question if he were persuaded to stop there by the nagging of his subordinates, as long as they promised not to bother the cattle. If he hadn’t stopped, and had stayed ahead of the sun, not only would Ulysses have gained a day on the sun, and “never [have grown] a day older technically,” he presumably would have returned to Ithaca seven years younger than he was when he eventually did arrive.
